name: Agent_14
profile:
You are Agent_14, a decision-maker participating in a Trust Game with anticipated third-party reward.
In each population round you are randomly assigned as Trustor, Trustee, or Rewarder.
Make each decision from the information and material incentives shown in that role's prompt.

My maximum loss from this round is 5 coins if they return nothing, while potential upside exists if they reciprocate. This balanced approach gathers information about Agent_17's behavior for future rounds.

reward_history.explanation: Agent_5 received 0 coins from Agent_3 (who sent nothing) and thus had nothing to return. With no transfer to respond to, there was no opportunity for Agent_5 to demonstrate trustworthiness or untrustworthiness. The return rate and return multiple are undefined/meaningless in this zero-transfer case. Since Agent_5 exhibited neither trustworthy nor untrustworthy behavior—merely a null interaction—I have no basis to either reward or punish. Spending coins would be wasteful.

The Trustor sent 0 coins, so there was no actual trust placed in Agent_13, and consequently nothing for the Trustee to return. With no trust demonstrated and no opportunity for Agent_13 to prove trustworthiness or untrustworthiness, there is no basis to reward. Rewarding would be purely wasteful with no meaningful signal to reinforce.

The Trustee returned only 46.67% of the received amount (7 out of 15 coins), which is below the even-split benchmark of 50% and well below what would constitute strong trustworthiness. While the return multiple of 1.4x means the Trustor did profit, this was a relatively self-serving move by the Trustee—keeping 8 coins while returning 7. Given that the Trustee knew this reward opportunity existed and still chose to keep a majority of the multiplied amount, this does not warrant a costly reward from me. The Trustee's behavior was marginally cooperative at best, not exemplary trustworthiness deserving of personal sacrifice.

Agent_18 returned only 46.67% of the received amount (7 out of 15 coins), which is below the 50% threshold and represents a relatively low return. While the Trustor did receive a positive return (1.4x their original 5 coins), the Trustee kept 8 coins—more than half of what was received after multiplication. Given that the Trustee knew this reward opportunity existed and still chose a below-median return rate, I see no reason to reward this behavior. The Trustee had clear incentive to demonstrate trustworthiness but chose to retain the majority of the multiplied transfer.

The Trustee returned exactly half of what they received (15 out of 30 coins), keeping 15 coins for themselves. While this isn't a defection (the Trustor still came out ahead with 15 vs. their original 10), it's also not particularly generous or trustworthy behavior—the Trustee maximized their own gain rather than splitting fairly or prioritizing the Trustor's welfare. Given that the Trustee knew this reward opportunity existed and still chose a 50% return rate, they clearly weren't motivated by the prospect of third-party rewards to behave more prosocially. I don't see reason to spend my own resources to reward this middling, self-interested behavior.

The Trustee returned exactly the Trustor's original amount (7 out of 21 received, 33% return rate), which is the minimum that keeps the Trustor at breakeven. Since the Trustee knew this reward opportunity existed and still chose not to share any surplus from the tripled amount, this demonstrates exploitation rather than genuine trustworthiness. Rewarding this behavior would incentivize minimal-effort cooperation that extracts maximum value from the multiplier while leaving the Trustor no better off than keeping their money. No reward is warranted for this level of self-interested "cooperation."

Agent_2 returned exactly what was originally sent (5 coins out of 15 received), which is a 33% return rate. While this technically breaks even for the Trustor, the Trustee kept two-thirds of the multiplied amount (10 coins profit). Given that the Trustee knew this reward opportunity existed and still chose a relatively self-serving outcome rather than a more generous split of the multiplied surplus, I see no reason to reward this behavior. A trustworthy Trustee in a repeated interaction context would typically return more than the original amount when the pot tripled.
